Over the years, the microfinance landscape has undergone transformations spurred by vari- ous financial sector platforms and policies implemented by different administrations. Microfinance products, including savings, loans, and remittances, cater to lower-income customers and restrict access to mainstream financial services (Aboagye & Anong 2020; Azmi & Mohamad 2024). The primary sources of financing for microfinance organizations include subsidized loans and grants from aid agencies, multilateral banks, and foundations (Jasmi 2021; Appiah-Kubi 2020; Asongu 2024). Deposits also play a crucial role in providing financial resources for microfinance institutions. Research has shown that these institutions con- tribute significantly to strengthening the financial system by facilitating lending and sav- ings transactions to support SMEs as well as promoting financial inclusion and financial sustainability and alleviating poverty (Kanake & Mahesh 2018; Audu et al. 2021; Ngwa 2019; Sultonovich 2023; Sulemana et al. 2023; Asongu et al. 2024). In recent years, emerging economies such as Ghana have undertaken effective and suc- cessful reforms aimed at bolstering their financial systems (Dick-Sagoe 2020). Financial deepening, which involves improving financial instruments, markets, and intermediar- ies, is critical for projecting a nation’s economic growth trajectory (Yang 2019). Against this backdrop, it becomes imperative to determine the fate of microfinance institutions within this evolving environment. The relationship between financial depth and economic development has been sub- ject to global debate (Botev et al. 2019). While financial development is often associated with economic growth, contrasting views suggest a negative relationship between finan- cial stability and sustainable development (Nasir et al., 2019). Microfinance institutions (MFIs) play a pivotal role in facilitating access to finance and other essential services, particularly in Ghana (Odoom et al. 2019; Appiah-Kubi 2020). However, access to finan- cial services for impoverished individuals is hindered by factors such as cost, risk, and convenience (Tambunlertchai 2018). Microfinance institutions face challenges such as segmented markets, dispersed popu- lations, and underdeveloped infrastructure, resulting in higher costs and limited engage- ment with conventional systems (Non 2023). Nonetheless, the sector has experienced significant growth in recent decades, with the number of participants soaring from a few thousand in the 1970s to over 130 million in 2012 (Nordjo 2018). However, expanding outreach, establishing a robust policy framework, operating microfinance institutions effectively, and ensuring financial sustainability remain pivotal for their success (Des- salegn 2018). Further research is warranted to identify critical variables for achieving financial sustainability, aiding microfinance institutions in sustaining growth and effec- tively combating poverty in Ghana. Tia et al. (2023) reported that, according to the National Financial Inclusion and Development Strategy (2018–2023), 58 percent of adults in Ghana had access to formal financial services as of 2015. Interestingly, Akuoko et al. (2021) reported that approxi- mately 80% of Ghana’s economically active population is engaged in the informal sec- tor. Paradoxically, this significant segment of the population lacks access to financing. In response to the profound impact of poverty in Ghana, since the 1980s, successive gov- ernments have implemented medium-term national development policy frameworks. A ppiah‑Kubi et al. The Economic Recovery Programme (ERP), initiated in 1983, was supported by targeted initiatives such as the Programme of Action to Alleviate the Social Consequences of Adjustment (PAMSCAD) and Ghana Vision 2020. Unfortunately, these programs fell short of their intended goals (Boateng et al. 2015). Despite praise for microfinance institutions (MFIs) in Ghana for promoting financial inclusion, sustainability, and poverty alleviation, there remains a limited under- standing of their true impact. Despite the proliferation of MFIs, a significant portion of the population faces obstacles in accessing formal financial services, hindering their economic participation (Dzansi 2019). Moreover, concerns persist about the long-term viability of microfinance operations and their ability to provide lasting benefits to clients while maintaining financial stability (Adams & Braun 2015). Additionally, the extent to which MFIs contribute to poverty reduction among vulnerable and marginalized popu- lations is unclear and requires further research (Ayentimi et al. 2020). Thus, a compre- hensive examination of MFIs in Ghana, considering their impact on financial inclusion, sustainability, and poverty reduction, is imperative. This analysis will offer valuable insights for policy formulation and enhance the effectiveness of microfinance initiatives in the country. The research seeks answers to the following inquiries: 1) What are the key elements that determine the financial viability of microfinance organizations in Ghana? 2) Does enhancing the financial sustainability and financial depth of microfinance organizations lead to improved poverty reduction in Ghana? 3) Does the financial sustainability of microfinance organizations in Ghana contribute to the enhancement of their financial deepening? To answer these questions, this research seeks to examine the interplay between financial deepening, financial sustainability, and poverty reduction in Ghana, utilizing the most comprehensive dataset available. By employing both the fully modified OLS (FMOLS) and dynamic OLS (DOLS) estimation approaches, this study aims to estab- lish the long-term equilibrium relationship between microfinance and other variables. Notably, the research adopts the logit technique to account for the enduring impacts of variables on poverty alleviation. Additionally, the correlation between access to financial services and poverty alleviation will be examined, alongside an assessment of the prob- ability of microfinance organizations’ influence on poverty reduction. By addressing gaps in previous studies and assessing key determinants of microfinance sustainability, pov- erty reduction, and financial deepening, this research aims to contribute significantly to the understanding of microfinance’s role in fostering sustainable development and pov- erty alleviation in Africa, particularly in Ghana. Literature review Antecedents of microfinancing Microfinance can be defined as the provision of financial services, such as insurance, savings and loans, to individuals with modest incomes in developing countries (Anwaar et al., 2022). It involves small-scale financial services, primarily credit and savings, for individuals engaged in various activities (Ademola Abimbola et al 2020). The finan- cial sustainability of microfinance institutions (MFIs) is assessed through factors such as financial viability, monetary sustainability, institutional viability, and borrower fea- sibility (Wondimu 2022). Operational self-sufficiency (OSS) is defined with respect to Gonfa (2019) as the total financial revenue divided by the sum of financial and operat- ing expenses. MFIs are evaluated in two stages: operational sustainability and financial autonomy (Khan & Shireen 2020). The financial sustainability of the microfinance sector is a debate between welfare advocates and institutionalists, with the Welfarist technique focusing on ensuring long-term financial stability and the Welfarist approach prioritiz- ing the breadth of effort over the depth of poverty reached (Leite et al. 2019). Institution- alists argue that creating a sustainable financial services sector for the poor should be a primary objective of microfinance (Deb 2018). Welfarists and institutionalists: theoretical underpinnings The financial sustainability of microfinance is a topic of debate among welfarists and institutionalists. Welfarists prioritize the breadth of effort, focusing on the number of people served, over the depth of effort, which refers to the height of poverty that is A ppiah‑Kubi et al. Institutionalists argue that microfinance aims to foster economic development by creating a viable financial services sector for the poor (Purkayastha et al. 2020). They argue that to effectively reduce poverty, large amounts of financial resources must be used, exceeding donor funding. However, MFIs must oper- ate efficiently and profitably to obtain assistance (Quartey & Kotey 2019). Welfarists emphasize their commitment to helping the most vulnerable but are hesitant to pursue financial sustainability because of potential misguided paths (Alexander 2018). The insti- tutionalist approach is chosen because of its long-term viability, considering the magni- tude of need and irregular donor money availability (Velte 2023). Excessive focus on fast strategic actions is seen as the second most viable option for providing financial assis- tance to impoverished individuals. In light of the narratives above, irrespective of whether welfarist or institutional theo- retical underpinnings are considered, there are common practical and policy concerns that emerge, especially with respect to (i) the factors that determine the financial sus- tainability of institutions; (ii) the impact of financial sustainability and financial deep- ening on poverty reduction; and (iii) the impact of financial sustainability on financial deepening. These are the primary objectives of the present study. This gap highlights the necessity of examining the financial, operational, and structural aspects critical for MFIs to attain sustainability (Asongu et al. 2024; Won- dimu 2022). The discourse highlights considerable involvement in the informal sector; nonetheless, the extent to which microfinance institutions effectively mitigate pov- erty for these individuals remains ambiguous. Addressing this gap corresponds with the second research question about the correlation between financial sustainability, depth, and poverty alleviation in Ghana. While global research has explored the relationship between financial sustainability and financial depth, few studies in Ghana have specifi- cally investigated the impact of sustainable microfinance practices on the financial deep- ening required to facilitate extensive financial inclusion and poverty reduction (Kanake & Mahesh 2018; Dzansi 2019). Investigating this impact is essential for formulating a microfinance institution framework that enhances both individual and systemic finan- cial well-being in Ghana, as related to another research objective. Although specific studies highlight the beneficial impacts of MFIs on financial stability, few empirical stud- ies have employed sophisticated estimation methods to ascertain long-term equilibrium correlations between microfinance variables and poverty indicators. This gap neces- sitates the application of methodologies such as FMOLS and DOLS to evaluate these dynamics, with the direct aim of comprehending the long-term effects of MFIs on pov- erty and financial sustainability (Diaz-Serrano & Sackey 2023; Adams & Braun 2015). Despite several legislative initiatives aimed at enhancing financial access, persistent diffi- culties in engaging marginalized communities indicate deficiencies in policy frameworks that may more effectively bolster MFI sustainability and outreach. Investigating this gap might enhance the formulation of more effective policies and regulatory frameworks for microfinance institutions, hence augmenting their contribution to poverty alleviation in Ghana (Dzansi 2019; Addae-Korankye 2020). Discussion of results The primary objective of this research is to identify the determinants of financial sus- tainability in Ghanaian microfinance organizations. The empirical research reveals that financial deepening, operating expenditures on the loan portfolio, net loan portfolio, and yield on gross portfolio are the key determinants of the financial sustainability of microfinance organizations in Ghana. This result aligns with the findings of other studies (Eke et al. 2018; Sari 2024; Wang et al. 2023; Bansah & Adjei 2023; Eze et al., 2016). The findings demonstrate that the reach of financial institutions, as measured by the total loan portfolio relative to the number of active borrowers, is a more effective method for forecasting financial sustainability. When financial institutions provide loans to bor- rowers, the process promotes financial depth and encourages inflows for the institutions via interest payments on such loans. Financial institutions charge borrowers’ interest in loans, which this research has proven to be a prerequisite for increasing the inflow of resources into the institution. The loan portfolio is another crucial component that con- tributes to the financial viability of microfinance firms. Other studies have supported this finding (Agasha et al. 2020; Bitok et al. 2020; Blanco-Oliver & Irimia-Diéguez 2021). The main idea here is that institutions may have implemented effective repayment arrange- ments that may successfully recover loans supplied to borrowers, thereby enhancing their financial condition. The institutions may use the group loan scheme to oversee and mitigate the risk connected with their credit portfolio. Furthermore, it assumes that the social components of loan assessment, which enable the categorization of borrow- ers’ credit risk, function flawlessly inside the microfinance institutions in Ghana. Cull and Morduch (2018) further support the idea that a strong loan portfolio is necessary for generating significant profits. This is because a strong loan portfolio allows for the charging of higher interest rates, which in turn contributes to financial sustainability. This research has identified the average number of loans per active borrower as a cru- cial metric for the financial sustainability of microfinance organizations in Ghana. This finding indicates that they adhere to the global banking standard of USD307 per bor- rower, which is quite promising. The measure of operating expenditures per loan port- folio serves as an indication of financial sustainability. Therefore, it has been shown that enhancing efficiency in the operations of microfinance organizations promotes financial sustainability. The institution under investigation effectively manages waste, resulting in loan administration and recovery cost savings. The findings align with the findings of CGAP (2005), which also indicate that reducing the cost of credit or expenditures related to loan or credit approval is a significant element in increasing financial sustain- ability. This research suggests that microfinance institutions use information technology to lower the expenses associated with extending loans. The use of information technol- ogy has resulted in a reduction in staff expenses related to loan issuance and processing. Appiah‑Kubi et al. Moreover, while addressing the second research question, the findings demonstrate that the financial viability of microfinance organizations does not have a positive effect on reducing poverty in Ghana. The financial deepening of microfinance organizations is necessary to alleviate poverty in Ghana. Microenterprises in Ghana have been una- ble to use financing facilities provided by microfinance banks to reduce poverty. With respect to the number of loans held by microfinance organizations, this metric is not advantageous in combating poverty in Ghana. The effective management of operating expenditures in the loan portfolio has played a significant role in poverty alleviation by microfinance banks in Ghana. Limitations and future research suggestions To ascertain the connections between the variables taken into account in this study, future research may additionally consider MFIs spatially. This will assist in evaluating the factors’ heterogeneities with respect to ownership, age, growth stages, location, and MFI product distribution systems. Furthermore, even though the focus of this study was pov- erty, financial sustainability, and financial deepening, other crucial factors, such as credit risk management and staff productivity or efficiency indicators, might be added to con- firm their dynamics. Thus, various facets of the sustainability of Ghana’s MFIs (missions, programs, and human resource sustainability) might be investigated in future stud- ies. The study’s limitations also serve as corresponding directions for further research. Moreover, due to data constraints, (i) the methodology relies heavily on aggregated financial metrics such as the average loan balance per borrower without considering some nuanced socioeconomic factors that influence poverty (e.g., the Gini coefficient or poverty headcount ratio). Hence, future research should incorporate data on borrower demographics, economic activities, and longitudinal poverty trends to strengthen the validity of these conclusions. (ii) The small dataset and generalized modeling approach may not adequately reflect the nuances of the relationship between financial sustainabil- ity and the capital structure of MFIs; thus, future studies should employ a larger dataset and more robust econometric techniques (e.g., panel data models with random effects) to yield more accurate insights into how capital structures influence sustainability. JSON: Name: mfi_fin_sustainability_ghana Title: Panel FMOLS/DOLS analysis of how microfinance operational and portfolio factors determine financial sustainability and poverty reduction outcomes in Ghana Short Hypothesis: An increase in depth of outreach (measured as average loan balance per active borrower) causes an increase in financial sustainability (measured as operational self‐sufficiency) of microfinance institutions in Ghana. Related Work: Existing empirical work on MFIs has predominantly used panel econometric techniques (unit‐root tests, panel cointegration, FMOLS/DOLS, VECM, and Granger/Dumitrescu–Hurlin causality) to study links among financial deepening, MFI performance and poverty. Two strands dominate: (1) institutionalist analyses that emphasize revenue, portfolio quality and operational efficiency as drivers of MFI sustainability; and (2) welfare‐oriented studies that emphasize outreach and depth as drivers of poverty reduction. Common methodological limitations are small and unrepresentative MFI samples, reliance on aggregated MFI financials rather than borrower‐level outcomes, weak identification of causal directions (cointegration and Granger causality provide association but limited exogeneity control), limited treatment of cross‐sectional dependence and spatial heterogeneity, and scarce use of robust endogeneity correction (IV/system‐GMM) or randomized/quasi‐experimental leverage. Studies also rarely jointly model MFI sustainability and poverty outcomes with consistent long‐run estimators plus robustness to alternative poverty and depth measures. Abstract: Problem: Microfinance institutions (MFIs) aim to balance financial sustainability with poverty alleviation, but empirical evidence on which operational and portfolio factors causally drive sustainability and whether sustainability translates into poverty reduction is inconclusive. Approach: Using a balanced panel of Ghanaian MFIs (2000–2019, MIX Market), we employ panel stationarity and cointegration tests, estimate long‐run relationships with FMOLS and DOLS, perform dynamic causality testing (Dumitrescu–Hurlin), and compare with fixed/random effects and system‐GMM specifications; we test robustness across alternative measures (depth, breadth, OELP, portfolio yield) and sample splits. Contribution: The study provides (i) rigorously estimated long‐run elasticities of financial sustainability with respect to depth, portfolio size, operating cost per loan and portfolio yield, (ii) causal direction tests linking sustainability, deepening and poverty outcomes, and (iii) robustness checks including endogeneity corrections and ablation by donor funding and spatial strata. Expected outcome: Precise, policy‐relevant quantification of which MFI levers most strongly affect sustainability and whether sustainability improves poverty outcomes in Ghana. Experiments: Datasets: Balanced panel of 11 Ghanaian MFIs reported to MIX Market, annual observations 2000–2019 (n=11, T=20). Variables: financial sustainability (FSS: operational self‐sufficiency or total assets/net liabilities+equity as used in source), financial depth (FD: gross loan portfolio per active borrower; alternative: private credit/GDP), net loan portfolio (LP), operating expenses per loan portfolio (OELP), portfolio yield (YP), poverty proxy (POV: aggregate dollar value of loans to poorest borrowers or alternative national poverty headcount where available), plus MFI fixed attributes and year dummies. Preprocessing: winsorize extreme outliers at 1st/99th percentiles; log transform positive variables where appropriate; test cross‐sectional dependence (Pesaran CD), panel unit roots (ADF‐Fisher, PP), and cointegration (Pedroni, Kao). Baselines: pooled OLS, country/time fixed effects, random effects, FMOLS, DOLS, and system‐GMM (Arellano‐Bover/Blundell‐Bond) with lagged instruments; for poverty outcome use panel logit and FMOLS on continuous poverty proxies. Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates, robust standard errors, t‐statistics, p‐values, long‐run multipliers (FMOLS/DOLS), R2/adj‐R2, AIC/BIC, RMSE for out‐of‐sample one‐step forecasts (where applicable), and area under ROC curve (AUC) for binary poverty regressions. Causality: Dumitrescu–Hurlin panel causality tests for directional links. Robustness/Ablation studies: (a) compare FMOLS vs DOLS vs system‐GMM estimates; (b) exclude MFIs with >50% donor funding (ablation); (c) reestimate with alternative FD and POV measures; (d) include spatial fixed effects (region) and interactors (ownership type, profit status); (e) instrument FD with lagged regional credit growth and test 2SLS IV validity (overidentification and weak instrument diagnostics). Statistical significance thresholds: 1%, 5%, 10%. Report: coefficient tables, diagnostic tests, causality matrix, robustness comparison table, and pre‐registered analysis code (scripts) for replication. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data coverage and sample size: only 11 MFIs over 2000–2019 may limit statistical power and external validity; selection bias if MFIs reporting to MIX are nonrepresentative. Measurement error: aggregated MFI financials are imperfect proxies for borrower‐level poverty impacts; poverty proxy availability and comparability may be limited. Endogeneity and reverse causality: depth, portfolio size and sustainability may be jointly determined; cointegration and Granger/DH tests do not fully resolve endogeneity. Cross‐section dependence and unobserved shocks: regional macro shocks or simultaneous policy changes may bias estimates if not captured. Stationarity and cointegration mis‐specification: misidentified integration order or structural breaks may invalidate FMOLS/DOLS long‐run estimates. Identification limits: absence of credible instruments or exogenous shocks constrains causal claims. Generalization limits: results focused on Ghana and period 2000–2019 may not generalize to other countries or post‐2019 dynamics. Computational limits: system‐GMM with small N, large T may produce weak instruments or finite‐sample biases.
